utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We continue with the cross-examination by Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness D, we have stopped yesterday the -- when you took the uniform and you were sent to the -- your first assignment. Could you tell us where was that assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first assignment was at the checkpoint at the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: My shift lasted eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay as reserve policeman in Ljubija? From 29th when did your duties cease to exist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: About one month, I don't know. I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How many checkpoints were on the jurisdiction of Ljubija police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How many checkpoints did you serve on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So on April 30th you were on that one? On May 1st you were on that one, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 30th of April. Yes on May 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... on that checkpoint on May 1st?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, already I am seeing now for the second time on the transcript "previous translation continues", which means that you have asked a question before the translation of the answer from the witness has been completed. So please, again, I ask that you observe the pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening -- that is, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Was that on the -- was that on the evening on May 1st or the morning of May 2nd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Morning of the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you during that meeting and what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that I should not leave the house until he gets there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You have testified already that he had arrived shortly thereafter; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you the question again: Once you met him, what did he tell you and what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that the Serbs had taken over the power, that the Muslim and Croat policemen were sent home, that they were relieved of duty. And I don't recall telling him anything, but we went together to the Ljubija police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When did he sign that loyalty in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last days of May or the first few days of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: What did he do from May 1st until the end of May, beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He regularly discharged his duties like other police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So at that time, on May 1st, through the end of May or beginning of June, it is fair to state that Serbs, Serb authorities, have not taken control of police station in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Have you gone -- from April 29th to 22nd of May, have you gone at all from Ljubija to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly. As a civilian, yes. As a policeman, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did you drive your own car or you rode with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion in someone else's car.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And getting into the Prijedor, you had to pass through Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Notice any checkpoints in Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Were you stopped at that checkpoint in Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the procedure at that checkpoint once you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: They checked our documents and searched the car to -- for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the men manning that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Aziz Aliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So that was a checkpoint that was on the jurisdiction of Ljubija police station, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But before you came to Tukovi, you had to pass through Hambarine; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And there was also a checkpoint in Hambarine, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below Hambarine, closer to Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: What was the distance between checkpoints in Hambarine and Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that Mr. Aliskovic was in charge of that checkpoint too. You testified that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen when you were stopped in Hambarine on any occasion that Mr. Aliskovic was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Have you recognised any other men at checkpoint in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew them, but I don't recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm going to ask you the question, the question about their names. Have you noticed if there were any Serbs among men on checkpoint in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So there were no Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And there were no Serbs on checkpoint in Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let's distinguish. The checkpoint at Tukovi and the checkpoint below Hambarine were two separate check points.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was a checkpoint before Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And just to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Just to make sure, you have also said a couple of minutes ago, that there was about one kilometre distance between those two checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: The checkpoint below Hambarine and the checkpoint before Hambarine, on the other side, was one to two kilometres. The checkpoint below Hambarine on the other side, between Tukovi, was also about two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Were those men on all of these three checkpoints that you had to pass through uniformed, or how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there were a number of people wearing different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did they have, if you could enlighten the court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military, police, and civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When you said "military," what -- which military did they belong to? Which military did this men belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was already the Serb military, and I concluded that by the insignia on the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just make sure that we are -- I want to assist you here. You said earlier there were no men of Serb ethnicity to those -- at those checkpoints. And now you're saying there were men in various uniforms and those ones in military uniforms belonged to the Serbian army. That's a little bit of a contradiction there. Would you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The checkpoint below Hambarine, that means in the direction Ljubija-Prijedor which was manned by the Serb police and the Serb military. From that checkpoint, 1 to 2 kilometres across the Hambarine in the direction of Prijedor was a checkpoint manned by the police. From that checkpoint in the direction of Prijedor, there was a checkpoint at Tukovi that was manned by the Serb police and the Serb military. And what I forgot to say that between the two checkpoints, that is the checkpoint below Hambarine, there was police and military that belonged to the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I think there was so many checkpoints here and I have been there so many times, and I'm just losing witness, you know, where those checkpoints are. But this is very important. And with your permission, I would like to give him a map so he can just indicate on the map where those checkpoints were and who was where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If I may approach the ELMO so that I can indicate the road that he is talking to so that he easily could point them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a much larger scale than the rest; Ljubija, Donja Ljubija. No this is Donja, and this is Gornja, upper and lower Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this map I really cannot see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] [In English]... everything here, maybe I am just showing to you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis. Hold on a minute, Mr. Vucicevic. There is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we object. It appears as though counsel for Mr. Kolundzija may have crossed the line into testifying himself at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are very close to that, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will show you, this is a map and map is, on its face, neutral. Map does indicate it's bigger man than the learned counsel has presented. There is all these geographic entities on this map. I was barely showing the witness the road on that map so he can point to assist the Court. You know, but witness was looking here and he was looking on the ELMO and I said it's not on this map. Now it's on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but you cannot give the evidence. The evidence must come from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if the witness, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask the witness the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you see on this map now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please use the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: -- Donja Ljubija, Gornja Ljubija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, you have to go back because the interpreters are not getting your questions, and bear in mind that we are not trained in cartography.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, neither am I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can barely see this map, and the lighting is a problem. But since I know the road quite well, that is, the one between Donja Ljubija and Prijedor, I will repeat what I have stated. My checkpoint was at the railroad station of Donja Ljubija, at the bus station, that is. The next checkpoint was below Hambarine about 4 or 5 kilometres from the point where I was on duty. The next checkpoint on the far side of Hambarine was about 1 to 2 kilometres farther away, and one after that was in the direction of Prijedor at Tukovi, 3 to 4 kilometres away from the one below Hambarine, or about 7 to 8 kilometres from the checkpoint where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... into the reserve police, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: As a reserve policeman, you had to respond to emergencies; wasn't that part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably yes, but we didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... without being able to respond, you had to at least have minimal ability to read the maps of your own town, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, again, we are having on the transcript "previous translation continues" in respect of the last two questions, which means that you are asking your question before the translation of the witness' answer has been completed. There will come a time when the Court's patience will be worn, and you must try to cooperate because we are not getting the translation of your questions. So we are not getting the evidence. That's what it really means. Are you now wearing the earphones?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, please wait for the translation of the answers. Yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Would, please, Court direct the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the question, because the question was not complete. Just rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were admitted into the reserve police and you had to respond to the emergencies, and the part of those minimum abilities you had at least to be in a position to read the map of your community, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I know the map very well. I did not say that I was unable to read it, I just said that I could not see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were -- at some checkpoints, there were military men who were Serbs, and at other checkpoints, there were military men who were non-Serbs. Were those men, Serbs and non-Serbs, mixed on any of those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at my checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But that was not -- your checkpoint was not the one on the road from Hambarine to Tukovi that I was addressing, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but we also had mentioned my checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... brings me to another point. Do you know of any Serbs who have responded to mobilisation to JNA -- strike it. Do you know any Muslims who responded to mobilisation in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: A lot of them responded, wasn't it true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that many. There were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And some of them went to serve in Croatia, wasn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean to serve in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Serve their assignment in Croatia, if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time one could not go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: What is true -- just to correct the record, is it true that some Muslims who put on the JNA uniforms went to serve in Croatia? Is that answer -- what is your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean as military personnel, as soldiers to go to Croatia, to the front line?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And some of them had military ranks, lieutenants, captains?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And some of them stayed throughout the years of warfare in Bosnia, later in army of Republika Srpska, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, all those who responded, the majority that is, who at that time went to the front, after the return, did not go there any more. I know officers, captains, reserve -- from the reserve force who, after their return, took off their uniform and returned it -- that is, who no longer went to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... one or two or three that didn't do it but stayed all the way until Dayton agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So isn't it fair to say that on April 30th, that Serb authorities took over the power in town of Prijedor only, while in town of Ljubija, they didn't take over the power?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say that throughout month of May, there was a demarcation line or, you know, territory -- was known who controls which territory, which was marked by different checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately except for Ljubija, that is the settlement of Ljubija itself, not counting the surrounding settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... a few Serbian villages which are located southwest or west from Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they were to the south or the southwest, I wouldn't know but I can give you some villages such as Lyeskari, Miska Glava, those two localities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday, you said that late Drago Tokmadzic was from Lyeskari, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And that was a Serbian village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kalajevo is right next to Lyeskari, or rather it is 100 metres distance, yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And before the war everybody knew that, including yourself, that Mr. Tokmadzic was a man from the mixed marriage? His mother was Serbian and his father was Croat; wasn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But between Ljubija and Prijedor, there is village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And you already testified that those checkpoints that were on the line which was abutting the Serb-controlled territory were the checkpoints manned only by non-Serbs, that's correct? You already said it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is below Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You have also testified yesterday there was no incidents, no shooting, from either side, from April 30th through May 22nd; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the shelling of Hambarine, that's right, but the date, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You are a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and being a citizen, you have heard that Bosnia and Herzegovina were recognised by certain countries in the -- in April of 1992. Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Jog your memory if I suggest it was on April 6, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Were they any military activities and casualties between the various ethnic groups in Bosnia from April 6th through April 30th? And I'm referring to any other municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Those days, have you read newspapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Which newspapers have you read?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: May have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But you don't recall whether you ever, from April 6th through April 30th, whether you ever in those days took the Kozarski Vyesnik in your hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... from Sarajevo? It was the major daily paper from the whole state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution will object on relevance grounds. We are prepared to give the Defence counsel some leeway on cross-examination, but we fail to see how this has any relevance with respect to the specific charges for which Mr. Kolundzija is charged with respect to the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I can't help, Your Honour, when the shoe is on the other foot, everything seems so different. The Prosecutor has alleged there was a state of peacefulness in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the aggression of the Serbs -- of Serb authorities happened in the municipality of Prijedor on April 30th. I'm just testing that. That is in the indictment and that is in their Pre-Trial brief, and I'm just testing that premise. It's background, Your Honours. I would be happy if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are consulting. The Chamber is consulting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic, the Chamber agrees it is of some relevance to the case, but you are not to belabour the point. I mean you have been cross-examining now for over an hour. So will you please proceed and deal with this point fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can lead on these because this is a cross, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have you heard about the clashes, military clashes at Ravno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not at that time. Now I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: In April of 1992 you never heard of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... at Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Military clashes in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm directing your attention now to the time while you were a policeman, and that's May. You heard about military clashes in Sarajevo on 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You heard of military clashes in Tuzla on 13th or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: -- 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So it is fair to say there were military activities in all other areas of Bosnia by that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And isn't it fair to say that Prijedor was the centre of Yugoslavianism which was depicted by the famous slogan "Brotherhood and Unity" in the communist times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And perhaps that is the reason why you were not interested what was going on in the other areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because you couldn't believe that ever the shooting is going to take place in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I could not believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So the idea of brotherhood and unity did not break up completely, but that part of unity broke up, but brotherhood, perhaps some people in your community thought that Serbs and Muslims could still continue to be brethren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, that's -- it seems more a matter of comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has testified yesterday that there was a gentleman who was a military officer, police officer, that brought him food to Keraterm. And how am I going to, you know, going to get some leeway please to relate it, to put it in right perspective. Because it is -- witness here who can put it in right perspective. He lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, but the question is so long that I believe the witness will have difficulty understanding it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the question, and I can answer it. At that time it required considerable courage to refuse to sign that loyalty. Had I had the choice, I would have signed it too, but I never had that choice, which does not mean that all those who signed it were not, afterwards, thrown out and removed and dismissed from that same Serb police in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that were in the military did not have that fate. That didn't happen to them. They stayed in the military throughout; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to ask Mehmed Captain First Class from Donja Ljubija about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Just with due respect, the Defence will bring the captain to testify about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just look at my notes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any desires to become a policeman while you -- when you were a young man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever made ahead -- went ahead and made application to the police station to accept you as a policeman prior to this what had happened prior to the outbreak of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I finished doing my army service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what had happened with your application?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I simply handed it over. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Was that before or after you went to vocational school to become electrician?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I finished my army service in 1984, maybe 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to direct you to the question: When did you finish your vocational school to become an electrician?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1982, 1983 is when I completed the training. I know what you want to ask me. You can go to do your military service until the age of 27, and you could go to a six-month course and then become a regular policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: This is a third time I'm coming to this question: When did you become an electrician?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When you applied to be a policeman, was that your first choice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned 1984 to 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to direct the witness to answer the question. The question was rather simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was: "When you applied to be a policeman, was that your first choice?" What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. My first choice was the business, the art of electrician. I said that in 1982-1983 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour -- it's in the record. We have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When -- while being interested to become a policeman, have you heard that police in those days were beating people while in their custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So when did you hear the phrase that in order to be admitted for the medical treatment that you have to say instead, "Police had beaten me up," instead, "I fell off the truck," or "... fell from the car." When did you hear that phrase?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded when in the camp itself that it was better to say that you'd fallen off a vehicle rather than you had been beaten. And I also heard from other inmates that that was better than -- a better answer than the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When you were in the camp, there were no trucks, there were no cars there, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it wasn't only when you had to go to the hospital, it was for all occasions. If a guard asked what was the matter with you, it was much better to say that you'd fallen than that you'd been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You used the word "fallen." When you testified yesterday you said when you were taken out, first you said you were hit and you fell, and in cross-examination, you said that you lay down, that you didn't fall. So which is true? Or explain what's the difference between laying down and falling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to lie down, you have to fall down first. Depends on the situation. If one goes to bed, then one lies down of his own will, but if on such an occasion, one lies down to the ground, then it must mean that he fell down. One can also fall down of his own will, that is lie down of his own will, but if one is first hit, then he will fall and then he will lie down. But I didn't lie down in the sense that you mean. I crouched. Rather, I lent -- I leaned against a wall to protect at least one side of my body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is a very important point because the witness is using inconsistencies in his testimony which do not have any explanation so far. I think you know that it's him to explaining how did it all happen. It's very important because it bears on credibility of entire testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will assess the credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You were hit by Dusan Knezevic, Duca. How tall was he when he was standing in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stood underneath. That is, I was on the threshold of the door at the time when he hit me. He could be, I should say, one metre 80, one metre 90, give or take a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: He is up at one metre 90? Knezevic is one metre 90?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could it be that he is 175?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. I didn't measure him. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... numbers are not important. The important is when he stood below --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do you ask me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When he stood below you, how far up to you did he come here? You can just show. Was he up to your chin, up to your chest here? How high was he up to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to my chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So when he took the baton to hit you, which hand did he hold that baton in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And could you just point exactly what part of the head did he hit with -- did he hit you on, with one finger, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So the baton went, as you showed, horizontally, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So that means the hit was hard indeed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: What that means, sir, is that he beat me good, that I was all battered up. And I am not the only one who speaks about that. Quite a number of people who were in the same room with me know about that. And I cannot tell you exactly, but I can describe it, if the Honourable Court permits me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... standing here and in deep sympathy what had happened to you. I think any --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you sympathise with me, you would have spared me such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm merely trying to establish what had happened, because at the time, sir, even being a witness or perhaps being innocently accused, it is a function of this court to examine the facts, and facts are words which are logically connected, and when you testify, with all sympathy to all what you went through, it is still important to remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, will you please spare us the speech and continue with your cross-examination? And try to bring it to a close as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So you -- if you don't remember how he hit you, you don't remember how you fell down, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember it well, how he hit me and how I fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Were you standing up when he hit you? Or you were beginning to already lay down? You were in the process of kind of lowering yourself down? In which position, standing up or you are slowly going down as he was taking a swing at you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I show it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness stands up] When we were called out, or rather when we were told that four men should come out --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness should show, not just give a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but he has to be able to explain what he's showing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For it to be intelligible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was standing in the doorway. Duca was in front of me. He hit me with his baton here. I turned and fell down next to the open door and I leaned against a wall and I was in this position, and he then continued to hit me on the head. From time to time I would manage to shield my head with my hands but then he would beat me here. And from different sides, others approached and kicked me in the head, around my kidneys, in the stomach, on the chest. And I had a feeling that Duca was talking to someone and beating me with his baton on the head as I was -- as I went into the crouching position and then, as I -- and then as I lay down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a visual and dramatic explanation. Let us see whether we can conclude this part of the evidence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How big was -- you're a big man.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could we just have a closed session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Or a private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Only for one minute, quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. Re-examination, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness D, in response to questions from Mr. Rodic, the Defence counsel for Dosen, you indicated that both Damir Dosen and his brother were known by the nickname of Kajin. Do you recall testifying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify, when you were at Keraterm, you testified that Kajin was a shift commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which one of the Dosen brothers were you referring to as the shift commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Damir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And is that the person that you saw in the courtroom and identified yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, the time when you were being beaten and you called out for assistance, your testimony was that you called to Pilip and Kajin to come to your assistance. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the person that you testified came to your assistance was, in fact, Kajin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which Kajin were you referring to who came to your assistance at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to Damir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that's also the person that you identified and recognised in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness D. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness D, that concludes your testimony. You are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before calling the next witness, could we go into private session very briefly? Because I'm going to be making an application for this witness to be given protective measures even though he has not been part of the application for protective measures earlier. The reasons therefore unfortunately will have to be in private session, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just one other comment, if I may, and that is that it may be that counsel may want to refer to other witnesses on the list by name. It's the familial relationship that causes the damage. In other words, we haven't edited out the names of people, because the names of people mean nothing unless people know that certain of those names people are, in fact, witnesses here. So if reference to their familial status could be avoided in the course of reference to them, I believe that many of the redactions wouldn't be necessary and we may also be able to conduct more of these in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is Witness E being brought in? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please show the witness a document that is now being handed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, I'd like you to look at that piece of paper. Do you see your name -- don't tell us what it is -- but do you see your name on that piece of paper and your birth date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And you see that behind your name and birth date that you will be referred to as Witness E; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might this be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness E, I understand, sir, that you are of Muslim ethnicity, and you were born at a small village near Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: While you were still very young, I understand you and your parents moved to Prijedor; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You completed your schooling, and after your schooling you worked for about four years in a furniture shop in Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you did your compulsory military service with the JNA, and you were discharged from that on the 5th of September when you became a member of the reserve until 1983; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Just a small correction regarding the date. It's 5th September. The rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought I had said that. But until the 5th of September 1979. And then in 1983, because of an injury to your arm, you were declared incapable of further military service and you were no longer in the reserve as well; is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand, sir, you went to work as a welder in Croatia for a number of years until 1991 and then you returned to Prijedor where you were on the 1st of May when something happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On the 1st of May 1992, sir, I understand that you were in Prijedor when the Serb forces took over control of that town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you knew that the police station and all the important buildings, including the railway station and government buildings had been taken over by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, that was announced on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do I understand, sir, that when that was completed, there would be a Serbian flag flying over the building as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you say you heard it on the radio. Was it also on television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We could rarely watch television. There was -- there were power outages, but we could transistor radios when we had batteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, prior to the takeover, sir, is it fair to say that the ethnically mixed community would live peaceably side by side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And there were many mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand that changed after the takeover; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, about a month later, towards the end of May 1992, I understand that you and your brother were taken into custody; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the people that took you into custody were dressed in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What kind of -- did you recognise any of the people that took you into custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did not know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection to the question. It calls for speculation. If he didn't know them, he wouldn't know their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us about listening to the radio. Did you receive any instructions via the radio announcement as to a manner in which one could show loyalty to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They told us on the radio that we should wear a white armband around our left arm and that would show the loyalty to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you were being arrested, sir, could you tell whether you and your brother were the only people being arrested or was it happening to neighbours as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They gathered us all, all of us who were there. They said that we should take our jackets with us, that we would be there for questioning for two or three days and then we would come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And could you see what was happening to some of your neighbours as they were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. After you were arrested, were you transported somewhere, and if so, on what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They gathered us from your homes and made us run down, followed by these transporters, to the buses. When we came to Osmana Dzafica, soldiers said, "Pull out everything you have in your pockets, as well as watches and jewellery and money," and some of them were hit there. And we were transported -- they put us in buses, and that is how they transported us to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you personally as you were being placed on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: One of them, a soldier, had a hunting rifle. He said, "Open your mouth." I did. And he put the barrel in my mouth and he pulled the trigger, but the -- it was empty, and he said, "Don't be afraid, don't be afraid. It's empty."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How did you react to that incident at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, nothing -- I was scared but I was calm. Had I made any move, who knows what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, how many people were being gathered and placed on these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: About 150 to 200 people. We did not count, so I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you recognise -- did you know the people that were being gathered along with you and your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. These were my neighbours. We knew each other in this local commune. Almost all of us knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This local commune where you lived in, I take it that's sort of a neighbourhood or a suburb of Prijedor, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And was it mixed ethnicity in that commune or neighbourhood, or was it largely dominated by one particular ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The majority of the population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And these people that were being herded on to the buses, do you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You said you went to the military barracks; where are those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It was at Urije, on the road to Bosanska Dubica, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, this location that you named, is that also still in the area of Prijedor or is it outside of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It is all the territory of Prijedor, as Donja Purharska, the local commune is, the Urije. This area was called Urije from as long as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I appreciate that and it's my question that's at fault. I understand that there is an opstina Prijedor which takes in a whole large territory with lots of villages, and then there is the town of Prijedor. Was it within the town of Prijedor, this location that you mentioned, the military barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The centre of town is what we are referring to as town, and the edge of town was the settlements that were about two and a half to three kilometres away from the barracks. Later they renamed it Prijedor 1, 2, 3 and 4. Donja Purharska was Prijedor 2, and I don't know exactly where Urije was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. When you went to the military barracks, did you get off the buses or did anything happen there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We -- at that time, we did not get off the buses. They were waiting for us and then they took us to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On the same buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how long did it take to get to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know exactly. I cannot say because in that fear, we did not know where we were and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was Omarska far away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It is about 18 kilometres away from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the buses drove straight to Omarska, did they? And by that I mean they didn't stop along the way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, they did not stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you got to Omarska, were you let off the buses, or what happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They told us to wait and then some people came and said that we couldn't go there because Omarska was full and they had to take us back, so then they took us back. They took us back to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you say "back to Keraterm," do you say that because Keraterm is on the outskirts of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. That is near the sign which marks the city limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So Prijedor is on the inside of the city limits of Prijedor on the way to Banja Luka; is that fair to say? I'm sorry, I meant to say "Keraterm."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I understand that you arrived at Keraterm still the same day that you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, we are talking about the 31st day of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What happened when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: When we arrived they told us to get off the buses and then they lined us up against a wall, made us lean against a wall, then they searched us. There were a number of men, I don't know how many -- I don't know how many men were searched at the time and when one group was done, then they would call another and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And at the time you were searched, did anything happen to you or the people who were with you being searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They searched everyone. I had nothing on me. A fireman had a small knife so they started beat him. "Is this what you're going to use to beat Serbs?" I don't know what else they were saying to him. But later on, they gave him what they were calling a special treatment. I think is what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we come to the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the break and resume at 11.30. Witness E, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness E, we -- just before we broke, you were telling us that you had arrived at Keraterm. Do I understand correctly, sir, that after you were searched, you were placed in one of the rooms at Keraterm? Do you remember which room you went to first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It was the largest room there, straight ahead. A large room that you walk in, walk into directly with a big door, and to the left there was another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And how long did you stay in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We stayed there for about 15 or maybe 20 days, I'm not sure, until they interrogated us. And after we would be interrogated, then they would move to us a different room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Might the witness be shown a photograph, Exhibit 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps, Witness, if I could have your attention directed to photograph 2B. First of all -- I'm waiting for the image to come to the ELMO. All right. First of all, do you recognise the scene in that photograph, sir, as something that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Indeed, that is Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And this first room that you were placed in, you say the one that was the largest room, do you see that in this photograph that you identified as being of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you take the pointer, please, and show Their Honours, please, which of the -- or where the room is that you were first placed in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And then you were -- you say you were interrogated. And after you were interrogated, you were placed in yet another room; which room is that? Would you point that out for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Right, it's this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You are pointing to the room that has the large doors immediately to the left side of the building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And the first room you were placed in was to the right of that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Right, yes. Except that this is a different door. It didn't look like this then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. By the photograph now, the doors look different now than they did in 1992; is that what you're telling us, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The location of the rooms are the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, that is all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know when you were there, did you know these rooms by any particular designation such as a number, for example? Did you refer to them by any number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Later on when four rooms were set up, then they became Rooms 1, 2, 3, and 4. At first only this larger room existed, but later on all these others were set up and those who were interrogated were taken to Room 1, and after a certain period of time to Room 3 too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. So this first room that existed, the larger room, what did that eventually become known as?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just so that I'm clear, the very first room that you went to, the larger room, the one that you say was to the right of the first room, what did that become known as?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That was later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So a room that was later on referred to as Room 2, that's where you went first, then were you interrogated, then you went to Room 1; is that correct? Do I understand you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you stay in Room 1 for the balance of your detention at Keraterm or did you go to another room later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Later, no, I didn't spend most of my time there. I -- the longest period of time I spent in number 4. That was a room that was turned into a military prison, mostly for Serb soldiers, that is, who had got drunk or done something, and that is where they were kept. But then later on, because we were too many, because the first two and the third room were overcrowded, then they put us in Room 4, and the military prison was transferred behind the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, you went to Room 4. You were there with a number of other prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You talked about the rooms being overcrowded. How many prisoners were in the room that you determined to be overcrowded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, this large one that we referred to as number 2, it had some 500 or -- men in it. I mean, one couldn't really breathe properly because people were sweating, perspiring, there was no ventilation, there was nothing. And as they were bringing in other people, it was getting more and more crowded. They had to open another room then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How about the conditions in Room 1, in terms of being crowded? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Much better. The conditions were much better because one could open the door, so that we did not have any problems of that kind there. One could breathe easier. It was much better when compared to the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were there any particular kinds of prisoners housed in these different rooms? In other words, were the prisoners in Room 1 different from the prisoners in Room 2 or 3 or 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- they were, the first two rooms, number 1 and number 2, that is first number 2 and after interrogation, people will be put in number 1, and as they were bringing in new people, they began to transfer them. And then suddenly they began to bring in people from Kozarac, and so they opened number 3, and that was overcrowded and they were transferring to Room 1, to Room 2, to 3, and then they had to empty that depot, and then they transferred the prison behind and they again sent us there. That is, they asked us who wants to go there. And then we did apply to go to that room, my brother and I, and some others. We said we would go there. I mean, to Room 4. And that is where we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, sir. While you were at the camp, can you tell us whether anything happened at the camp to the prisoners, that you could see or hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What kinds of things did you see or hear happening to prisoners while at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They had made a penal group. There were some pallets as you entered Room 2; three, four, five pallets. And when I came, yes, they would take it out on various prisoners, doing to them all sorts of things. That is how -- what it was like in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to ask you to be specific about doing all sorts of things. What do you mean when you say they were doing all sorts of things to prisoners? What did they do to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Beat them, and what do I know. That little Car was killed. It was Duca and Ziga. They beat him with a rifle and the machine-gun somewhere on the road to Bosanski Novi, and he was caught there and they wanted him to show them how he had carried this machine-gun. They forced him to run with it and then to crawl with it. And then they were beating him. And at some point he simply fell down on the ground, and then Duca and Ziga hit him with their feet all over the body. And then he was lying on the ground, and then they took him -- he was carried into one of the rooms, and the next day he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see this incident yourself, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did, yes, because it was right opposite the door and the door was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was this in the daytime or at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Daytime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Who did you see beating him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I saw Zigic and Duca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know Zigic from before your internment at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: For a while we were together involved in youth brigades and then he became a taxi driver and I worked in the field. And at times when I would see him there, when I came into that town, then I would ask him to take me to a hotel. If I went to the hotel, of course, I would pay the fare to him always. He lived in Cirkin Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How about this man that you referred to as Knezevic? Do you remember his full name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't. I don't even know him. I mean, I did not know him before. I only could hear them say or shout out, "Duca is on his way."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you see Duca participate in this matter as well, in the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The two of them did it together, he and Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was it only Zigic and Duca or were there other people involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly because nine years is not a short period of time. The two of them simply stuck in my memory because I saw them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, I heard you make reference to a machine-gun and crawling. I'm not quite sure exactly what you said about that. Perhaps you could indicate to us what you saw in relation to what Car was doing while Duca and Zigic were beating him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They gave him a machine-gun to carry and run in a circle carrying it. And after that, they told him to go down on his fours and to crawl with it around, with that machine-gun. And as he did that, they beat him and kicked him and yelled at him, "How you've come here to kill Serbs," I can't really remember their words they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'm going to turn to another incident. In your stay at Keraterm, did you become familiar with the names or did you know any individuals by the name of Banovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did not know them personally before. I only heard that they were called Banovics in the camp and that they were twin brothers, but they were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How -- were you able to tell them apart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were there some unique features about any one of them that allowed you to tell them apart?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. One of them had long hair and was nicknamed Cupo, and the other one had short hair and had an earring. They were not all that alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So from that statement, do I assume that they were not identical twins but fraternal twins, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. They were fraternal twins, that is what I heard. I do not have any knowledge of that, but their likeness was not all that big. I mean one couldn't really say immediately that they were twins.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to an individual by Cupo that you referred to. Did you see him do anything to anyone while you were at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He was the one who beat. He had a baseball bat, and he beat some prisoners from Kozarac. And then once as we went for lunch, he took out a knife and pricked him in his left leg, in his left thigh.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Maybe I don't understand your answer, but you said he took out his knife and pricked him. To whom are you referring when -- who did he prick with the knife, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. An inmate. I don't really know who that was, because there were people whom I did not know, whom I'd never seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that that knife incident happened while people were on their way to lunch, or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Right. That is, if one can call it lunch, because we would get something to eat only once a day around 7.00 in the evening and we called that lunch. So it was on our way to lunch when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, while we're still talking about Cupo, did you know someone by the name of Jovo who was also with you in Room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did not know him before, because he lived somewhere up in Ljubija so that I did not know the man. But he was brought to the camp, and they put him in Room 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened to Jovo, if anything, while you were in Room 4 with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. Did something happen to Jovo that you can tell us about today, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know when it was when they called him out, but I think he was a very short time there, and the same day he was brought in there they called him out. He went out and they beat him, and beat him, and beat him. And after that, they put him back inside, and I think it was the same Cupo Banovic who had called him out. And then they shouted, "That is how we punish Serb traitors."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Where was Jovo beaten, in terms of location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I couldn't see it all, but they were beating him from between number 1, that is where they had taken him and then all the way down to number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you personally see this beating, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I saw Banovic hit him with that baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: As a result of that beating, do you know what happened to Jovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I think that he died shortly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know someone with a nickname of Faca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yeah. That is, I didn't know him. I never met him so I don't -- I don't know him. I don't even know what his real name is. But since he came to the camp at Keraterm, as he would come, somebody would point a finger at him and say, "What's up Faca?" "Faca come over here," and then he would slap somebody in the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was Faca an inmate of the camp or was he a visitor or a guard, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He came to the camp from time to time, and at times he also came with his dog there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when he came to the camp, apart from slapping people in the face, did you see him do anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did not see him do anything else. But I heard from a friend who lived in Brezicani that he had killed his relative, that is, this friend of mine told me that he had seen him kill him in the -- in a lavatory, but I did not see that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When this Faca came to the camp, you told us that he would sometimes slap people in the face; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How often did he come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I couldn't really say. He did not come all that often, perhaps a few times. Well, not a few, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not trying to press you on the matter, sir, but sometimes we don't know what "few" or "several" means. Are you able to attach a approximate number to "few" or "several", or if not, I'm not asking you to speculate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, several times is when I -- I mean, four, five, six times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And apart from slapping people in the face, did you see him do anything else in relation to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's been asked that question and he's already answered it in the negative. He did not see him do anything else, which is at line 11:53:06.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It matters not. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just returning, if I may, to one thing that I forgot to ask you when we were talking about Jovo. You gave the opinion that you think he died. What drew you to that conclusion, sir? What did you see or hear that led you to the conclusion that Jovo died from that beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: We saw that he was not breathing any more and took him out to the left from our door to a pallet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Did you know a police officer from Ljubija in the camp by the name of Drago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know if anything happened to him while he was detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He was detained for a while and then one night they called him out, or rather evening. At night-fall he was called out. I don't know who exactly called him out. It could be Banovic, but I can't really say. Banovic was one of them. And they took him out and beat him. We barely heard him. All we heard were blows. And something clinking, like a rifle or something. And one could hear that baseball bat hitting something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You referred to the name Banovic. You don't know if Banovic did the beating. Do you know whether Banovic was there or do you know whose shift it was on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, not really. Banovic was there. But now I just cannot recall -- I can't remember which shift it was. I think it was the shift that Crni was in, but I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. When you referred to Banovic and the baseball-bat sound, which Banovic are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Cupo, Cupo. Yes. His brother did nothing. He just sat up there and did nothing. He did it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what happened to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
