utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, the witness earlier said, I think it was the shift that, is it, Crni was in?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe he used the word "Crni." I'm going to get to Crni in a couple of paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm still on 10, about to move to 11, and Crni is referred to in 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions, sir, about Drago. Do you know what happened to him after this beating? Do you have any personal knowledge of --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. He died after he was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, you could see the man was turned all black and blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did he come back into your room after the beating but before he died?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He didn't come back. He was carried in, back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Who carried him in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I think that they called out some four inmates to carry him through the door into the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you saw he was dead, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: After, after -- well, it all looked to us like a minute or two but it could have been half an hour, 20 minutes. But at any rate, he died shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do I assume that his body was taken out of the room and taken away after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's right. All of those who died were taken out to the left of this room and put on a pallet. There was one next to a door, and that is where they were put, and then a small truck would come from the public utilities company, and took them away. Where, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you. Sir, are you also aware of a person who was ethnically Albanian who ran a cake shop in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I had heard that he was of Albanian ethnic background. I could hear his accent when he was speaking, and I knew that he had a pastry shop, and he was there with me in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did something happen to him, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He was also taken out, beaten. They used all kinds of objects on him. He had scars on his head. There was blood. But -- and then shortly thereafter, he died, so there was no more blood after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know who beat him or who was present or what shift was on during that beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The shift where the most beatings took place was the one where the Banovic was, and this Keli and Crni. It was mostly during their shift that the most beatings took place, and we were most afraid of that shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you've just told us that's when it usually happened. What happened -- are you able to tell us whether or not -- which shift was on when the Albanian gentleman was beaten to death?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I think -- I didn't know this name, but I knew him by the nickname of Crni. "Crni" means dark. He was not very tall. He may have been about 170 centimetres tall, well-built, short hair. He was always wearing a short, black T-shirt, and he had a nickel-plated pistol with nickel-coated bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. Your Honours, I anticipate that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 during the course of the next discussion there may be a quote which will -- might identify someone. I'd like to move into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that. I would have carried on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps allow me to rephrase my question earlier about Duca. You told us that he came to the camp from time to time, and I asked you when he did -- on those occasions when he did come to the camp, what would he do? I think you told us that he came with somebody, or did I get that wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They were coming, and Zigic would come with him and some others. There was one with a red beret, I don't know who he was, and several others. They would come in a jeep or some other vehicle. They would always come at dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And without getting into specifics in answer to this question, when they came, what would happen, in general?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He took Fajzo and he said, "Who killed my brother?" He asked Fajzo. And he told him, he said, "You put my brother's head in a vise and kept tightening it until he died." And then they brought Fajzo's wife and child and told him, "We'll kill them both if you don't tell us." And then he cried and he said that he didn't do it, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Maybe I can get a couple of details. Do I understand correctly that on one of these occasions when Duca came to the camp, he had dealings with a man that you refer to as Fajzo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see Fajzo's wife and child at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. She was holding it in her arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did anything happen to Fajzo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Duca came, took a knife, and he sort of cut him across the knife [as interpreted]. Then we bandaged him. I don't know how much he cut him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You referred to, I believe you said, a punishment group. How many people were in that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That group kept changing. There weren't always the same people in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And this group you're referring to, were those inmates in the group or are you talking about perpetrators, people who did things in the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That was a group of inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right, sir. And I think I'm going to move on. Do you know what happened to Fajzo? Did he stay at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He did not stay at Keraterm. He was called out. I don't know whether he was sent to Omarska or somewhere else. I don't know exactly. Sometime they would call out people and say that they were going to Omarska, but we did not know where they would end up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So you know he was called out, but you don't know what happened to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to turn now to an incident. Do you remember something that happened to the inmates of Room 3, latter part of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. We were sleeping. It may have been 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning. I don't know exactly. We could not orient ourselves. We did not have watches so we did not know what time it was, but -- we could not know the precise time. But we could hear a song, a Serbian national song, and suddenly we could hear shattering of glass and something, words to the effect, "Don't run." I don't know who said that. And then it started, the shooting, first several shots, and then bursts of fire. I don't know what weapons were fired. That I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You were in Room 4 at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's right next door to Room 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. There is only a wall separates them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did anything happen, during the course of this gunfire you heard, to anyone in your room, Room 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. One young man was hit in the arm by a ricochet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know what type of prisoners were being housed in Room 3 just before this shooting incident you've referred to? Do you know where these people were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. They were from the area of Hambarine, Carakovo, Biscani, the area up there. This is an area called Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do you know how long those people had been at Keraterm before this shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I think six to seven days, perhaps. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know someone at Keraterm by the name of Kole, the nickname of Kole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what was his position at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He was a shift commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Referring to the night of the shooting incident, do you recall anything that would lead you to believe whether or not Kole was there or not there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly whether he was present there during the shooting, but when the shooting was going on, he said, "Stop shooting. Fuck your mothers." Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know this Kole before the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I used to know him. Not that I was very close to him, but I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How long had you known Kole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In what sort of circumstances did you know Kole? Like were you at particular locations when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I think that he played soccer for Cirkin Polje, but we also had a club ourselves so we played them, and so I knew him through these soccer teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift was on, and if so, how do you know about that shift being on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That was Kole's shift, because he would come at 10.00 p.m. and lock the door, and this is how I know that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see Kole at Keraterm that evening before the shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, he came to take over the shift. The shifts were taken over at 6.00, 6.00 a.m. or 6.00 p.m., so one shift was from 6.00 to 1800 hours and the other one 1800 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One other question about that, sir, and that is you think that you heard Kole's voice. Is there something about his voice that would allow you to recognise it if and when you heard it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He has a somewhat, I don't know, rough voice if I can -- actually, it's a bit rough and a bit high-pitched.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, after the shooting incident, did something happen the -- in the morning hours of the day following the incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In the morning they collected the dead bodies and they placed them to the left, which is the place they would always put dead bodies before taking them away. I think this was done during the Banovic and Crni's shift. Later on in the evening, I don't know what time it was exactly, they took out a group of people. They beat them there, and they killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, they took them out of Room 3. This is what we were told later. We knew that it was not from Room 4, Room 2 or Room 1, so it must have been from Room 3. They brought them out they were crying. They said, "Don't. Don't." And suddenly shooting started, and later somebody started shouting, "My leg. My leg." And then you could hear shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, were there some people in your room, sir, who were involved in the aftermath of the shooting incident on the first incident? Let me be more specific. Do you know an Aco and Sekerin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Aco and Sekerin, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. What did they do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They were carrying the dead over there. This is what we learned three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did they tell you about how many bodies there were after that first shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I heard, according to their accounts, that there were 127 killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did they also tell you how many were wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. They told us but I cannot recall the exact number. I think that there was about 57, something like that. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Or 47. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, you've told us that the following day, if we want to call it that, in other words, there is a morning shift and you said that people were being taken out, and then later on you told us that there was an additional number of people who were being beaten; is that correct? Do I understand you correctly that later the following evening something happened further to Room 3 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The first shooting was during Kole's shift. The second shooting was the very next night, the night after. When the night came, they brought them out. Later on I learned that it was 22 men dead, that they brought out, beat them, and then killed them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you hear that information from Aco and Sekerin as well or from someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: These were the men who had stayed in Room 3 who said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you've told us that you knew Kole before the conflict and did you talk to Kole a few days after the shooting incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you remember what Kole told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He said to me, "I think -- had I been there, nothing would have happened."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you say you knew Kole before the war. And do you think that you would be able to recognise this individual if you were to see him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you look around the courtroom now, sir, and if the person that you've referred to in your evidence as Kole, if he's in the courtroom, could you point him out, please, and tell us where he's sitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: To my right at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. You are pointing in the direction of -- to your right, did you say? Could you hold up your right hand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: To the right from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He is at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You are looking to your left and holding up your right hand, which is the opposite hand. Perhaps you could point at the individual so that Their Honours can see where you are pointing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It's the one at the very end by the corner over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You are pointing to the back wall of this courtroom or to the wall. There are six seats, for the record, in that back wall. There are three policemen and three people in civilians. Can you tell us which chair, counting from left to right, the person that you refer to as Kole is sitting in? Counting from left to right including the police officers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The fifth chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, identifying Kole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, did -- were you ever allowed to use the telephone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I asked Kole if we could call home after that to just let them know that we were all right, and he let us do that. So we went to make our calls and we called our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you were making these calls, where was the telephone located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It was in that room next to the weigh bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit 2 again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask that the usher show the witness Exhibit 2C.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: First of all, sir, do you recognise the photograph now shown to you marked Exhibit 2C in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is that the room or weigh -- by the weigh bridge to which you have referred to in the foreground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You earlier told us that, I believe, that when you were taken to be beaten, you were -- this is the place where the commanders were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you go to this particular hut, that is the one with the flat roof and the white -- in the foreground of the photograph 2? Is that where you were taken to use the phone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you take your pointer, if you would, please, and tell us where the phone was located and what did you see near the phone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Here, inside, next to this glass where it opens, that is where the telephone was, and next to the telephone were the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see any lists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did. There were all the lists, the lists for all the four -- for all four bedrooms, dormitories.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, were all the prisoners given the right to use this telephone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Who do you know -- are you able to tell us how many prisoners were allowed to phone home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I know that my brother and I used it. I don't know how many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. And you and your brother knew Kole before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know about my brother. I know that I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know someone by the name of Kajin or someone referred to by the name of Kajin while you were at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I knew him for quite sometime before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Had you had any dealings with an individual by the name of Kajin before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Once we got into a fight at the railway station. He and his colleague were involved. I don't know who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you remember what the fight was about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. He was refusing to pay for the use of the lavatory to a woman who was there, and we started an argument. And we had all had a drink or two, so we got involved in a fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you see this person with whom you had been in a fight at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sometime during your dealings with this individual at Keraterm, did he make reference in any way to your previous encounter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: When I saw him there, I hid inside for the first two or three days. I was afraid. I dare not come out. But then he called me out and said, "Listen, I'm not one of those who will go for tit-for-tat. Nobody will touch you. But I do know that you carried a rifle in the SDA call it attack on Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did he indicate anything to you about what would happen to you if you had belonged to a particular group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you describe Kajin for me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. At that time he was younger than he is today. And he was rather thin, tall, blond, dark-blond or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you say you knew this man before the war. How well did you know him before the war, apart from this fight you had with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say how long, because he's younger, and we were not often in the same company, but when we went swimming, we'd go together or would be in the same place, I mean hotels. I came across him at various places.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How often did you have dealings with him at Keraterm? How often did you see him, apart from this conversation with him that you've just related to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: What do you mean, "often"?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's something I'm going to have to ask you to describe for us. On how many occasions would you say you saw this person you refer to as Kajin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He was the camp commander in the early days, in the beginning, so that we would see him every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you think that you would recognise this individual today if you were to see him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you please, then, look around the courtroom, and if the person you've referred to as Kajin is in the courtroom, could you point him out, please, and tell us where he is sitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He is in the middle, next to -- one, two, three, the third seat from left to right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Third seat left to right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: For the record, again, identifies Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you've made reference to people that you say were in a special punishment group and referred to Duca. Do you recall any incidents involving those inmates where Kajin was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I think he was there when Car was killed. I believe he was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did Duca or Zigic ever appear while he was on shift, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, they did, but I just don't know how many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you remember any one incident that you know Kajin was present and, if so, how you know he was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, once they took out the man who is called Kocijas, who was nicknamed Kocijas, and another guy. It was sometime in the evening. I wouldn't know the exact hour. And forced the two of them to fight between themselves, that is to deal blows to each other. And as they were doing this, a soldier or somebody came up and said, "Stronger, stronger," and then hit one of those and said, "This is how you deal a blow." And that was it, and then he laughed and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Who laughed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My question is: Who laughed when the prisoners were forced to beat each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Kajin was laughing. Kajin was laughing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know an individual by the name of Sikirica while you were at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I never knew him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you know someone by that name while you were an inmate at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I only knew him by nickname, that is what I had heard, that his name was -- that he was called Sikirica, that he worked at Celpak, and that he was a shift foreman. That is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did this individual that you later heard to be referred to as Sikirica ever tell you what his function was at the camp? Did he personally tell the inmates that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. When he came he said, "I'm the new camp commander." That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you ever see the individual that you refer to as Sikirica involved in beating of any of the prisoners while in your presence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you remember whether people were beaten while he was on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Usually when the Banovic group was there, that is Banovics and that Keli and Crni. They were usually the ones who beat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you describe this gentleman that you knew as Sikirica for us, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, he wore a military uniform, very smart, well-ironed, military boots, and at that time, he had a mustache, thin mustache, and short hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And how often would you say you saw Sikirica in the camp during the period of your detention, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: From the beginning every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you feel that from your seeing this man at the camp, having him tell you he was camp commander, and seeing him nearly on a daily basis, you would be able to recognise him if you were to see him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you look around the courtroom and go through the same procedures as you did for the other individuals, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It's the second one from the left to right. The second seat with the beard. Now he has a beard. He didn't have it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And again, that's in the back row as I'm looking at the courtroom to your left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. I can see him directly from here, but there is also a guard before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might the record show that he's identified the accused Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, what can you tell us about conditions at the camp after Sikirica told you that he was the new camp commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Nothing. It could only get worse. It couldn't get better. Because we could not have from the beginning, we could not have any protection afterwards. We had no protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very briefly, sir, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about camp conditions. You've already told us about food. Very briefly, what kind of food and how often would you be fed, and how were the conditions about getting to and from the food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, the food wasn't anything to write home about. We had one meal a day. In the beginning it was a little earlier. Later on they moved it on to 7.00 in the evening, and there wasn't enough food for everybody. There wasn't food for everybody all the time. At times when Banovics, and Keli, and those others, when they were there, then we would be given 30 seconds to have a meal, and I don't think you can take a single bite in 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What would happen to you if you exceeded the time limit they said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, beaten, and they'd hit whoever they could lay their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How about the toilets, sir, were there sufficient toilets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. And they were all blocked at times. We tried to clean them. I mean one simply couldn't go in because of -- what do you call it that smell, that stench, what to call it. They were all flooded. At times when there was water, we washed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were there facilities for washing yourselves or your clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, we did not. No, we did not have that. At times during Kole's shift, we'd ask Kole, "Can we go? Is there water?" And then at times he would allow us and say yes. So on one occasion we all had a bath during Kole's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The water that was supplied or available, was that drinking water or was it -- well, was it drinking water or was it a different kind of water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: At times drinking water was brought in, cisterns, from the water supply company and the fire brigade. And at times we also used the water from the hydrant when there was no other water, when there was no other water.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did the prisoners develop any diseases to your knowledge or any gastro symptoms to your knowledge while you were an inmate? And by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "gastro" I mean stomach ailments.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Some contracted dysentery, that is, vomiting and diarrhea.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was the effect on your body weight while you were at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I lost 14 and a half kilograms during that time from the beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You arrived in Keraterm on the 31st of May 1992, and you left when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: On the 5th of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand you were taken to Trnopolje where you were eventually released on the 12th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I was released -- well, I'm not quite sure. Was it the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were you at -- let me ask this in two questions. Were you taken to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you stay long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Three or four days. Three, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you have to sign any documents in order to be released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. In order to be released, I had to sign over everything and to leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I just want to consult with my colleague and I believe those are my questions. I just want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So how long approximately would you say you stayed at Keraterm? Are you able to tell us that or we can do our own math?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Altogether, 68 days. I mean Keraterm and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Those are my questions. Would you answer my learned friends, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, I think we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was going to ask you to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness E, we are going to adjourn until 2.30. During the break you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody and that includes members of the Prosecution team. We stand adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.59 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness E, I'd just like to ask you quickly please about this: Is it correct that in relation to these matters, you have made two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, one in February, 1995 and a second in August of last year, 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is this also right, that when you made your second statement, you were able to go through the details of your first statement and to confirm that what you'd put in your first statement was accurate, with the exception I think of one minor detail concerning a member of your family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, may we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this, please, Witness E, you were in Prijedor at the end of April 1992. Is it correct that you, yourself, were not in employment at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: At that point, I did not work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Between the takeover of Prijedor by Serb-dominated entities and your arrest, were you able to move around the municipality in the ordinary way that you had previously been able to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was that because there were now some checkpoints manned by the military or the police which were checking identities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't even know that they were checkpoints. I just didn't feel like going down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So because of the change in political situation, you decided in large to remain at home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you hear of or witness any military activity or fighting in the Prijedor area at the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I heard -- I had heard some shooting, but I did not know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you were arrested on the 31st of May 1992 with, I think, about 150 others, would this be correct that the make-up of that group was, in essence, men of military age? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No, I do not agree. I was not able-bodied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The phrase I used was "men of military age" not military capability, Witness E, military age. Would you accept that? In other words, 16 to 60.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know what is the military age. There were men who were over 60, over 70. They could not have been of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Don't mention any names, Witness E, but is it right that you were questioned about the age of your father at the time of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you told the people who had come to arrest you that he was 60, and having told them that he was that age, they allowed him to stay, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And also left behind were your mother and sister. Again, don't tell us any names. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The -- some of the people who came to arrest you, you considered to be Chetniks, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean when you say "Chetniks"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, what you told the Office of the Prosecutor in both of your statements is that you considered some of them from their accents, at least, to be Chetniks either from Lika or Licani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I called them men from Lika. They had those accents and they had cockades on their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But the phrase you used to describe them, do you accept, was "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Having been arrested, you've told us of your various travels to various places, Witness E. Is this correct that it became evident when you were turned away from Omarska because there was insufficient room, it was evident, was it not, that no organisation had taken place concerning your group as to where you were going to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any preparations for that. I cannot conclude anything about that. They just gathered us up. I don't know if they knew how many people they were going to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were the people who were driving the buses to Omarska, were they surprised to be turned away? Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You couldn't see it or they weren't surprised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They just told them, "Go back," and then they just turned around and they went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Upon your arrival at Keraterm, is it right that you were searched, and one of the items which was taken from you was your identity card?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, and cigarettes and a lighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And were identity cards taken from all the other people who arrived at the same time as you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's right also that that identity card was returned to you whilst you were in detention at Keraterm; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is that true of the other detainees, they also had their identity cards returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Not all identity cards were returned to everyone. Some remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Without asking you to put a definitive, accurate figure on it, what sort of proportion of the people in the camp had their identity cards returned to them, Witness E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you say it was the majority of people had their cards returned or a minority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I do not know that. I know that my brother and myself had our identity cards returned to us. I don't know about the others. I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the process of you all arriving and being searched, one individual was mistreated. That was because he was found in possession of a knife; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: In fact, we have to make a distinction. There is a difference between a knife and a cakija.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell us what the difference is, Witness E, so we can understand your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Knife is bigger, you know what a knife -- and cakija is smaller and it falls, so it's something that you bring along in your pocket so that you can maybe slice an apple or cut some bacon or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In English I think we would use the word "penknife" to describe such an implement. Is that something that you would understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I thought that's what you meant. Is this correct also, Witness E, that initially, upon your arrival at the camp, there was no mistreatment for at least two or three days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly those two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If I was to refresh your memory from the second statement which you made to the Office of the Prosecutor, you told them on that occasion, "For the first two or three days, nothing happened to us." Does that refresh your memory, Witness E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Something like that. That's how it was approximately, even though we had been -- we were locked up so we were not in position to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like now to turn to some specific incidents involving individuals you've talked about. The Serb whose name was Jovo, you've told us what -- something of what was said at the time, but is this correct, that the motive for ill-treating that person was because he had either voted for the SDA or had displayed posters of the SDA or Alija Izetbegovic at his home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The people who knew him, who used to know him, and he was from Ljubija, they said that his -- there were SDA posters on his house, but I don't know whether this was true, but this is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the Banovic brother who assaulted him did so out of -- because he was wanting to take out his revenge and aggression upon Jovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know whether Banovic said that, but I heard that someone said later something like it. "This is how we punish the traitors."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The reason I ask you - and may I refresh your memory from your statement made in 1995 - is that you said to the Office of the Prosecutor, "Banovic who carried the baseball bat took out his revenge and aggression on him." Is that something that you were able to observe and conclude? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He beat him. And why he beat him, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Turning now, Witness E, please, to the man Drago Tokmadzic. Is it right that in relation to him, the motive for attacking him was because he was both Croat and an active police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You are not able to say who it was precisely who beat Drago Tokmadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I heard -- what's his name? This Banovic, whose nickname was Cupo, I heard him, his voice, and his baseball bat, which had that hollow sound when it delivered blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would this be correct, that the body of Drago Tokmadzic was taken away in a hearse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I think that they were all taken away in a hearse except those -- but we will come to that. Those who died individually were taken away in a hearse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I turn, now, please, to the Albanian, the man who owned the cake or ice-cream shop at the Prijedor station. Is this correct: That the motive for assaulting him was because he was believed to be wealthy, and there was an interest in extorting money from him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: There is a great possibility that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The man, Car, who was alleged to have a machine-gun when he was arrested, was that the focus of the ill-treatment of that man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is it right that that was an incident which took place at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They dealt with him during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from Jovo, you were aware of other Serb detainees, I think, in Room 4. How many were there who were detained in Room 4, Serb detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: With us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Either with you or later separately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: They were not with us. They were -- they were there when there were only Rooms 1 and 2 as military detention. They brought them there, men who either got drunk or did I don't know, and this is where they kept them. One of those who had beaten us when we were being placed on buses also ended up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you say, please, if you know, how many people were being -- how many Serbs were being detained at any one time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the issue of camp commanders, please, Witness E. During your stay, it's right, isn't it, that three separate people were commanders of the Keraterm facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The person who was commander of the Keraterm facility when you arrived remained in that position for some 25 days after your arrival; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Approximately that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So that person was replaced on or about the 25th of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The second person who was commander of the camp, was that person, in turn, replaced sometime around the 27th of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. We could not keep track of the -- of dates, and we could not orient ourselves in that respect. So I wouldn't be able to say exactly what date it was. We did not have a calendar. And we did not have watches in order to be able to see what date it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just so that we can try and fix it, if you will assist me, please, Witness E, you told the Office of the Prosecutor in your statement in 1995 that you had remained at Keraterm from 31st of May until the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: On the 5th of May. On the 8th of May [sic], I left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The 8th of May or the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And just help me about this: Is this correct that the change from the second commander to the third commander took place shortly after the incident in Room 3 and about a week before you were transferred to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That's all right. I'll do it again. Can I just refresh your memory from the two statements which you've made to the Office of the Prosecutor. What you've told them was that in relation to the change-over from the second to the third commander, that that event took place shortly after the incident in Room 3 when people were killed, and about seven days or thereabouts before your transfer to Trnopolje. Does that refresh your memory as to when the change-over took place, Witness E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: The first commander was there for about 20, 25 days. The second commander came after him, and the last 7 days, 7, 8 days something like that, that is when the third commander came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you learn the name of the third commander either at the time or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I only knew that he worked -- that he had worked in a shop. I don't know what his name was. Actually, a lumber yard. I know that that company was from Banja Luka, but I cannot recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If I suggested the name Marinko Sandzak to you, would that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know his name because I had not known him before. He did state his name and he told us that nobody would touch us while we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And so that third person was in command when you left for Trnopolje and supervised the closure of Keraterm and the transfer of prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Sikirica was also there with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But by that time, the man you had been told was Sikirica was no longer the commander, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He was no longer the commander, no longer. He had taken over that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Indeed, I suggest, and you must deal with it, Witness E, that at no time did he personally tell you or anyone else that he was commander of the camp. The only thing he may have said was that he was commander of security at Keraterm. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That is not true. When he came he said, "I'm the commander here."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Those were his words, "I'm the commander here." I'd like to move on, please, Witness E, to the punishment group or the special treatment group. Would this be correct that that was established by Zigic and Duca around the 20th of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I'll tell you one thing, I do not remember the dates and I couldn't know the dates, but this group was set up after three or four days, not after two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What you told the Office of the Prosecutor in August of last year, Witness E, was this: "Around 20 days after my arrival in Keraterm, the guards established what they called the punishment group." Does that refresh your memory as to what you've said in the past?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. The punishment group was not set up then. It was set up before, right after the arrival in the camp, three or four days later, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: And this group came into being right then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct, Witness E, that the focus of the perpetrators who were involved in that was against those firstly who were considered extremists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. They were not Muslim extremists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, again what you told the Office of the Prosecutor was that the basis for selection was those prisoners who were selected as extremists on their arrival in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you understand by the phrase "extremist" or the concept of "extremist," these categories of people: Those who were known to be members of the SDA or activists in the SDA, people who they believed were involved in military activity, and in particular people from Kozarac who may have taken part in resistance at Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that is what they called them. I do not know how they identified them. That young boy, that Kocijas, he did not belong to any resistance or any party, but allegedly he had killed a guy who was a Serb and that was why he was to be in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But the other type, the other categories of people, can you say anything to confirm that that was how they focused their attention? In particular, but not exclusively, on those kind of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I will put it to you again. Forget for a moment about the young man you've spoken about just now. Is this correct, that by "extremists" were meant, for example, people who were members of the SDA or were activists in the SDA, people who had taken part in resistance fighting or military activity, in particular people from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know what they thought. I don't really know who was a member of SDA or who wasn't, so I cannot say yes or no or why.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it right that many of the group who were part of the special treatment group were, in fact, from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But many of them were, weren't they, Witness E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, majority, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is it within your knowledge that Duca Knezevic also came from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't really know where he comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When you were interrogated, Witness E, can you help us about this: Was the nature of those questions about you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, they asked me who I am, what I am, where I was born, where I came from, where I'd served the army, if I had any weapons, if I carried any weapons, if I knew who carried the weapons, who sold the weapons, if I knew that there were weapons for sale, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct, that the people who were conducting your interrogation were what were known as inspectors who had come from outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't really know where the people -- where these people came from. I did know one of them, but I cannot place him really.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did they appear to be, as it were, professional policemen, used to asking questions in this way? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did the people who were interrogating you appear to you to be professional policemen, for example, used to interrogating people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know. They wore uniforms, but I just don't know what they were, policemen or military. I just don't know. But they wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: After people had been interrogated, Witness E, did that lead to those who had completed the process of interrogation being moved from one room to another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is this correct - and if you don't know the answer, please tell us - that the people who took the decision as to where people would be moved, those were the people who had conducted the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I didn't really understand that question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. The people who took the decisions as to whether you should be moved from one room to another, or indeed from one camp to another, did you understand that that was -- those were decisions taken by the people who had conducted the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: After the interrogation, they would move us from one room to another. Two or three days later, or perhaps even the next day, depends, some were called out to be sent to Omarska, to collect all their belongings and go to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to the matter concerning Room 3, Witness E, please. You saw none of the preparations for that incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. I was asleep at the time. I'd just fallen asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you subsequently, or indeed at the time, learn that the incident had been perpetrated by soldiers who had come from outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I do not really know who did that. I did not learn that. I do not know who fired the shots or what.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you learn anything of how many people had been involved in perpetrating that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: From what you were able to hear, Witness E, would you accept that it was at least one member of the Keraterm personnel who did what he could to prevent and stop what was taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I heard Kole shouting, "Stop, don't fight, fuck you, don't fire."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is this also right, Witness E, that you understood from what you heard that, in part, he had tried to prevent and stop what was going on by discharging a submachine-gun in the vicinity of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he fired or somebody else because I could not see that. But I could identify the automatic rifle because there is a difference between it and machine-guns or other rifles and then I thought that it could be him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that the shooting stopped after the intervention of Kole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And would it be right to conclude from that fact that the intervention that you had heard was therefore effective?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand what my friend is trying to do, but there is a point at which the speculation that's being called from the witness goes beyond his realm of knowledge. He's told us what he knows. What my friend is trying to do is get something that's for argument as opposed to witness' argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we agree. Please move on, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Witness E, that Kole, on other occasions, was responsible for preventing people who were not supposed to be at Keraterm from coming into the premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, I'm sorry. Could you rephrase it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. You were aware that Kole had, on occasions, prevented people from coming into the Keraterm facility from outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I must say I don't remember that, but I do -- I must say that during Kole's shifts there were no problems. We could sleep quietly and everything when Kole was on duty. And if somebody came and hit an inmate, then he would hit him and tell him to leave us alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this right, that you told the Office of the Prosecutor in August of last year that you remembered seeing soldiers coming to the gate of Keraterm seeking to come in, wanting to come in, and Kole turning them away and that he would swear at them and say that they would not come in whilst he was on duty; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that's right. Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And that on occasions, Zoran Zigic would be in the camp during Kole's shift, but he would not mistreat people during that period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He came as a visitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. And when he came during Kole's shift, Zigic did not perpetrate any mistreatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Kole did not allow any mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And during Kole's shift, the man Duca Knezevic would not come in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did not see him then. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help us about this, please, Witness E: Do you know or did you know at the time in 1992 of somebody called Zivko Knezevic? Does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just two bits of detail, please. The man you have identified as Dusko Sikirica, you didn't see that person ever carrying weapons whilst he was in the Keraterm facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help us about this: As far as inmates who were sick or unwell, was there anybody who you believed to be suffering from epilepsy, which you understood to be suffering from epilepsy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was it one person or more than one person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: More than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was one of those somebody called Nehru Garibovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Finally, these matters, Witness E, if you can help us, please. During the time when you were detained at Keraterm, how many people do you say were detained along with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I could not say, not the exact number. There were quite a number. Many people passed through that camp. I should say about 1.200, 1.300 maybe. I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would this also be correct, Witness E, that of those who passed through the camp, some were released completely to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: During the first fortnight, yes. After interrogations, some were released. After that, nobody was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you say how many people were released in that way during the first fortnight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: During the time when you were in Keraterm, Witness E, would you accept this: That all of the detainees were in the complete power of the Serb authorities throughout the period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Excuse me, did all?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the period that you were detained at Keraterm, would you accept that you and your fellow detainees were in the complete power of the Serb authorities who had detained you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And would you also accept that throughout that period, there was nothing that would have prevented those same Serb authorities from killing all of you en masse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I simply fail to understand the question. I am at a loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that those, the Serb authorities could, if they had wished, have killed all of you at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honours will just give me a moment, please. I have no further questions. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness E, I should first like to ask you to tell us briefly -- I'm sorry, I have some problems with my headset -- to tell us briefly what was life like in Bosnia in the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It was perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mean everybody lived peacefully, quietly, in harmony, regardless of the ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We can therefore conclude that that was the best time ever, at least in our memory, isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, the 80s.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that time you were convicted for slandering, for offending the former president Tito, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes. Tito was involved, but no, I did not insult his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, I was in railway station, in a pub, and we were sitting and drinking and there was a policeman with us. And they were singing some song, and I said, "Well, that's not really how it is, you -- it's like that." And he said, "What do you know about this song? What do you want?" Right. And he tells me, "Well, if you know the lyrics of that song, you sing it." And when he said that, I said, "Oh, fuck it. I've just forgotten it." And then he said, "Oh, so you are using foul language to speak about Tito and you this, you that." But I've never done that in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you told us that you were a member of the Liberal Party. I do apologise. You told us a while ago that you were a member of the Liberal Party, and just in a sentence will you tell us which were the -- what was the basic political doctrine of that party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: You mean -- well, I was just an ordinary member. I wasn't a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that you were a member, but you must have had a reason to join that party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Because everybody was in that, Croats and Serbs and Muslims and all the others, and that's why I was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is true that the Serbs took over the town of Prijedor without firing a single bullet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And it is also true that you heard about that, as far as I understood you, from the radio because the power had been cut off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I was with a friend who used to work for a bakery up there, and his name is Mladen Rabac, and he worked in a bakery, and I was with him, that is I visited him from time to time. He would just say, "Why don't you come over? Why don't you drop by?" And I did drop there and I was there until 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning because the bakery was open -- open only at night, and I was carrying some -- carrying rolls or something with me. And I saw some vehicles full of troops, but no plates, nothing, just passing by. What they were doing, I really don't know. But when I arrived home in the morning, then I learned that the SDS had taken over power in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So at that time, in Prijedor, the power had already been cut off, is it, was cut off or you began to run into trouble with power supply because you said that you had to use your radios because television was not working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true. There was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And in the months that followed, while you were detained in that Keraterm, there was no electricity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, at times there was; at times there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the frequency of power outings and the other, and when you had the power?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I can't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement that in pre-war Bosnia there were very many mixed marriages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And I should say around 70 per cent, isn't it; wouldn't you say? What do you think? How many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, had I ever got married, perhaps I would have known that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And it is quite true that in Prijedor people gave their children names regardless of whether their children were Serb? They were often given Croat names or the other way around? There were many such cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what kind of a name is Damir, whose name is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't sound like a Croat name to you, does it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I have a friend whose name is Jasmin and yet he's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, before the war, you all frequented the same places, you all socialised and were -- and kept company to each other, with some more, with some less, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you used to see Kajin at all those places where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Well, not at all the places where I went to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But at some places you frequented you also saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And at that time none of you rank and file people even dreamed of something might happen as what did happen a couple of weeks or couple of months later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Never. I didn't even know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just go into private session, please, for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The barracks where you were taken was at that time controlled by the Yugoslav People's Army or some Serb military forces, is that how would you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: That's what I already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you learn that Keraterm was used as a prison for Muslims and people of other faiths and ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: When I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you had never heard -- you had not heard about that previously. After you arrived at Keraterm, you were searched, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you did not know any one of those who searched you? Will you please -- you nodded but we need a verbal answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: People who searched you were not Keraterm guards, the ones that you would see later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I did not know them. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And later on you never met them, correct, if I understand you correctly? That is, in the subsequent two months, you did not see them there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. We had our backs turned to them. This is what we had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that time did you observe that some other military police or paramilitary unit was part of the security at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: At first some came to provide assistance at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were these members of the military police or members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I think that it was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know any one among these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, I knew one, Savo. He unfortunately died.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was their commander, who was their leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But I wouldn't be wrong if I said that they had their own commander or superior person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: It is possible, but we were not in a position to know who was doing what and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Today also, when asked by Mr. Greaves, you said - and you previously stated that too - that in the first days not much was going on in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: To some people nothing particular happened, but to those who were member of the punishment group, they did have something happen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say the first days, how many days do you have in mind, a couple of days, five, six days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: I know that it is different -- interpreted differently. A couple of days sometimes means two days, sometimes a full week, sometimes even ten days, sometimes -- so it refers to different time frames.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So people interpret differently what a couple of days means. To you what did a couple of days mean? Let's say in the situation when -- as when you mention it in your statement, what did you mean by a couple of days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Between two and five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I presume that upon your arrival at Keraterm, you very quickly learned that there were guards there, that they were organising some kinds of shifts; is that correct? Did you notice that in the -- that at first there were two shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would I be wrong if I said that -- that a person whom you called Crni was in one of these shifts, in fact one of the shift's leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know who he was and what he was. I didn't know whether he -- who was the shift leader there, and I didn't know what he was doing, but I knew that he was doing almost everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And along with Crni, you also saw Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS E
utterances.text: He and Zigic were there in the same shift most frequently.
